findings.title: nearby_moves takes the target user's id as a caller-supplied parameter and returns that user's RSVP status for every move in radius
findings.location: supabase/migrations/016_one_nearby_moves.sql:30 (param), :88 (my_status), :100-113 (crew_going); caller: src/hooks/useNearbyMoves.ts:20-28, :41
findings.reproduction: Get the victim's uuid: GET /rest/v1/public_profiles?username=eq.<victim>&select=id (view granted to anon at 019_profiles_exposure.sql:54; this is the same lookup useSearchUsers.ts:23-28 performs). Then POST /rest/v1/rpc/nearby_moves with the anon key from the app bundle and body {"lat":40.4406,"lng":-79.9959,"radius_m":50000,"uid":"<victim-uuid>","page_size":1000}. Nothing in the function body compares `uid` to `auth.uid()` — it is used raw at line 88 as `max(r.status::text) filter (where r.user_id = coalesce(uid, auth.uid()))`. The client already sends this parameter by name (useNearbyMoves.ts:25), so the wire format is exactly what the app itself emits.
findings.consequence: Every returned row carries `my_status` = the VICTIM's RSVP ('going'/'maybe'/'waitlist') alongside `latitude`, `longitude`, `address`, `location_name` and `starts_at` for that move. One request returns the victim's complete plan for the next 24 hours (016:126-127 bounds starts_at to now()+24h), metre-exact, for every move within 50km. `crew_going` (016:100-113) additionally returns who from the victim's invite tree and squad is going with them — so the attacker also gets the victim's companions. Blocking does not defend: `not public.blocked_either(m.creator_id)` (016:129) resolves against auth.uid() — the attacker — and only filters moves the victim CREATED, never moves the victim merely attends. Called with only the anon key, auth.uid() is null, `blocked_either` returns false for every row, and the block filter is inert entirely. This is the single query that answers 'where will this specific person be tonight' for a 17-25 user base (age hard-limited at 011_squad_safety.sql:34-42).
findings.fix: Delete the parameter. In 016_one_nearby_moves.sql: `drop function if exists public.nearby_moves(float,float,int,text,uuid,int,int);` then recreate with the signature `(lat float, lng float, radius_m int default 8047, filter_cat text default null, page_offset int default 0, page_size int default 50)` and replace every `coalesce(uid, auth.uid())` at lines 88, 102, 103, 106, 109, 112 with a bare `auth.uid()`. Then remove `uid` from the RPC body in src/hooks/useNearbyMoves.ts:25 and drop the `uid` argument from fetchNearbyMoves (:17, :48) and from the query key (:46). findings.extra: Enforcement layer: NONE. No RLS policy, no WHERE clause, and no assertion anywhere in the 21 migrations constrains `uid` to auth.uid(). supabase/tests/01_functional.sql:137-156 tests only that exactly one nearby_moves signature exists and that it returns the enriched row — it never checks whose my_status comes back.

findings.title: The rsvps table is world-readable, making it a direct person-to-planned-location index
findings.location: supabase/migrations/005_rsvps.sql:59-60
findings.reproduction: GET /rest/v1/rsvps?user_id=eq.<victim-uuid>&select=move_id,status,squad_with,created_at with the bundled anon key. The policy is `create policy "rsvps_public_read" on public.rsvps for select using (true);` — no `to authenticated` clause, no predicate, and no later migration touches it (grepped all of 006-020 for policies on rsvps; only insert/update/delete are re-stated). Then GET /rest/v1/moves?id=in.(<ids>)&select=title,location_name,address,starts_at,location_point — `moves_public_read` (004_moves.sql:77-78) is likewise unrestricted by role.
findings.consequence: A complete attendance history and forward schedule for any member, keyed by their uuid, plus `squad_with` — the explicit list of who they roll with (011_squad_safety.sql:5-6). This bypasses every function-level control the schema has: get_move_attendees' block filter, nearby_moves' 24-hour window, nearby_moves' radius cap, and the ban filter. It also makes the attacker's own footprint zero — no RSVP, no profile view, no report trail. Because the policy has no role restriction, the query works with the anon key that ships inside the app bundle, i.e. without an account at all, which defeats the invite-gated-network premise the whole product rests on.
findings.fix: In a new migration: `drop policy "rsvps_public_read" on public.rsvps; create policy "rsvps_read_scoped" on public.rsvps for select to authenticated using (user_id = auth.uid() or exists (select 1 from public.moves m where m.id = rsvps.move_id and m.creator_id = auth.uid()));`. Every legitimate client read of another user's RSVP already goes through a SECURITY DEFINER function that will keep working (get_move_attendees at 010_blocks.sql:158, my_rsvp_status at 006:3, waitlist_position at 014:16, nearby_moves' aggregate counts). One thing breaks and must be changed with it: the realtime attendee-count subscription at app/move/[id].tsx:43-51 filters `table: 'rsvps'` and will stop delivering to non-attendees — gate that useEffect on `isGoing || isCreator` (both already computed at :37 and :103) and fall back to invalidating queryKeys.moves.detail on screen focus for everyone else.
findings.extra: Enforcement layer: none — `using (true)`. Table-level GRANT to anon is the Supabase project default; 018_lock_internal_functions.sql:11-19 independently confirms against a live database that anon reaches public objects through the default grant.

findings.title: A block does not stop the blocked user from RSVPing to your move, and the roster filter then hides them from you
findings.location: supabase/migrations/005_rsvps.sql:63-64 (rsvps_authenticated_insert); supabase/migrations/010_blocks.sql:175 (`and not public.blocked_either(p.id)`); render at app/move/[id]/attendees.tsx:18-21, :38
findings.reproduction: A blocks B. B obtains one of A's move ids — from the world-readable rsvps table, from get_user_moves (see the finding above), or from any link A shared via app/move/[id].tsx:60. B POSTs to /rest/v1/rsvps with {move_id, user_id: <B>, status: 'going'}. `rsvps_authenticated_insert` checks only `user_id = auth.uid()` (005:64); no policy and no trigger consults public.blocks. B is now on the roster. A then opens /move/<id>/attendees, which calls get_move_attendees, whose body drops B because of `not public.blocked_either(p.id)` at 010:175.
findings.consequence: The block filter runs in the wrong direction on the one screen where the victim most needs the information. A is shown a roster and a header count "Who's going (N)" (attendees.tsx:38) that silently omits the person she blocked, while B has confirmed attendance at A's stated location and time. The count also visibly disagrees with `move.attendee_count` shown at app/move/[id].tsx:194, which comes from the unfiltered aggregate in moves_with_counts (005:130-134) — so the discrepancy is on screen but unexplained. For an app whose product is telling people where you will be, concealing a blocked user's confirmed attendance from the victim is worse than not filtering at all.
findings.fix: Two changes. (1) Stop the RSVP: add a restrictive insert policy in a new migration — `create policy "rsvps_no_blocked_insert" on public.rsvps as restrictive for insert to authenticated with check (not exists (select 1 from public.blocks b join public.moves m on m.id = move_id where (b.blocker_id = m.creator_id and b.blocked_id = auth.uid()) or (b.blocker_id = auth.uid() and b.blocked_id = m.creator_id)));`. (2) Change the roster filter from bidirectional-hide to blocker-only-hide, so the move creator always sees the full roster: in get_move_attendees (010:158-178) replace `and not public.blocked_either(p.id)` with `and (exists (select 1 from public.moves m where m.id = p_move_id and m.creator_id = auth.uid()) or not public.blocked_either(p.id))`.
findings.extra: Enforcement layer for 'blocked user cannot attend your move': NONE. Enforcement layer for 'blocked user is hidden from your roster': get_move_attendees (010:175) — enforced, but in the direction that harms the victim.

findings.title: The category the schema itself describes as "someone's place" is published to the public map at full coordinate precision with no way to make it private
findings.location: supabase/migrations/017_category_parity.sql:11 (just_us definition), :14; supabase/migrations/004_moves.sql:29 (`is_public boolean not null default true`); src/hooks/useCreateMove.ts:15-32 (insert omits is_public); src/types/app.ts:214; supabase/migrations/016_one_nearby_moves.sql:79-80 (ST_Y/ST_X, unrounded)
findings.reproduction: Open the Create tab, pick the '🛋️ Just Us' category from CategoryPicker (fed by CATEGORY_META, src/types/app.ts:214), long-press your home on the map to set the point (app/(tabs)/index.tsx:122-126), submit. useCreateMove.ts:17-30 inserts creator_id, title, description, category, location_point, address, starts_at, ends_at, max_attendees, cover_image_url, vibes — and no is_public, so the column takes its default of true (004:29). The move is now returned by nearby_moves to every caller in radius, with `ST_Y(m.location_point::geometry)::float` and `ST_X(...)` at 016:79-80 — no round(), no jitter, no snapping, at any layer between the geography column and the JSON response.
findings.consequence: 017:11 defines just_us as "small and private. A few people, someone's place, no crowd." There is no is_public toggle anywhere in app/(tabs)/create.tsx (grepped: the word does not appear) and no rounding anywhere in the schema or the client. A 17-year-old (the floor enforced at 011:34-38) hosting friends publishes their home address — `address` is returned verbatim at 016:71 and rendered at app/move/[id].tsx:186-188 — plus metre-exact coordinates, to anyone with the bundled anon key inside a 50km radius (app/(tabs)/index.tsx:68 caps radiusM at 50_000). The map draws a ~44px pin, which reads as approximate; the payload is not. The private-move machinery the RLS policy at 004:78 supports (`is_public = true or creator_id = auth.uid()`) is real and correct, and is unreachable — no code path can ever set the column false.
findings.fix: Two changes, both small. (1) Give the creator the switch: add `is_public: input.is_public ?? true` to the insert object at src/hooks/useCreateMove.ts:29, add `is_public: boolean` to CreateMoveInput in src/types/app.ts, and default it to false in app/(tabs)/create.tsx:51 whenever form.category === 'just_us'. (2) Round what leaves the server for anyone who is not going: in 016_one_nearby_moves.sql replace lines 79-80 with `case when max(r.status::text) filter (where r.user_id = auth.uid()) = 'going' or m.creator_id = auth.uid() then ST_Y(m.location_point::geometry)::float else round(ST_Y(m.location_point::geometry)::numeric, 3)::float end` and the same for ST_X — three decimal places is ~110m, enough to place a pin in the right block and not on the right doorstep — and apply the same conditional to `m.address` at line 71 so it returns null until you are actually going.
findings.extra: Enforcement layer for coordinate precision: NONE EXISTS at any layer. Enforcement layer for private-move address hiding: the RLS policy at 004_moves.sql:78 would enforce it correctly, but no client path can set is_public=false so it never engages.

findings.title: validate-invite is an unauthenticated, unthrottled oracle over a ~1M keyspace that returns the credential needed to sign up
findings.location: supabase/functions/validate-invite/index.ts:9-58 (no Authorization check anywhere; service-role client at :24-27; codeId returned at :52); keyspace defined by supabase/migrations/007_referrals.sql:29-37; consumed by supabase/migrations/015_security_hardening.sql:78-100
findings.reproduction: POST https://<ref>.supabase.co/functions/v1/validate-invite with body {"code":"MOVEAB23"}. The handler reads req.json() at :16 and never inspects req.headers for an Authorization or apikey value — CORS is `*` at :5. generate_referral_code (007:31-37) builds every personal code as the literal 'MOVE' plus 4 characters drawn from a 32-character alphabet, so the entire personal-code space is 32^4 = 1,048,576 candidates, and every member holds a live one with 5 uses (007:22, default_invite_allowance). A hit returns {"valid":true,"codeId":"<uuid>"}. Feed that uuid straight into POST /auth/v1/signup as raw_user_meta_data.invite_code_id — handle_new_user (015:82-96) accepts any code id whose use_count < max_uses and mints a full member.
findings.consequence: The invite gate is the app's only membership control and the entire basis of the closed-network positioning. It falls to a scripted sweep of one million requests with no account, no rate limit and no logging on the caller. That matters here specifically because it is the door for the one attacker this product cannot tolerate: someone who was deliberately not invited. Once through, every path above is available to them as an ordinary authenticated member — and the invite-chain accountability trigger (011:47-61, flag_inviter_on_ban) misattributes the intrusion to whichever real member's code was guessed.
findings.fix: Stop returning the code id, and make the code text the thing signup consumes. In supabase/functions/validate-invite/index.ts:51-54, return only `{ valid: true }`. In supabase/migrations/015_security_hardening.sql:78, change handle_new_user to read `new.raw_user_meta_data ->> 'invite_code'` (the text) and resolve it itself with `update public.invite_codes set use_count = use_count + 1 where upper(code) = upper(v_code) and use_count < max_uses returning id, created_by into v_used_id, v_inviter;`. Update app/i/[code].tsx:53-55 and the sign-up screen to carry the code string rather than a codeId. Separately, gate the function: add `if (req.headers.get('apikey') !== Deno.env.get('SUPABASE_ANON_KEY')) return new Response('Unauthorized', {status: 401})` at the top of the handler, and widen the code space by generating 6 suffix characters instead of 4 in 007:33 (32^6 = 1.07e9).
findings.extra: Enforcement layer: NONE. Compare supabase/functions/generate-invite-codes/index.ts:25-33, which does check a bearer secret and fails closed — validate-invite has no equivalent.

findings.title: get_move_attendees returns any move's full roster to any caller with no check that the caller may see the move
findings.location: supabase/migrations/010_blocks.sql:158-178; caller at app/move/[id]/attendees.tsx:18-21 (p_limit: 200)
findings.reproduction: POST /rest/v1/rpc/get_move_attendees with {"p_move_id":"<any move uuid>","p_limit":200}. The body (010:170-177) selects from rsvps joined to profiles filtered only on `r.move_id = p_move_id and r.status = 'going' and not public.blocked_either(p.id)`. It is SECURITY DEFINER, so the `moves_public_read` visibility predicate (004:78) and the `moves_select_not_banned` restrictive policy (011:143-149) are both bypassed — nothing in the function establishes that the caller can see this move at all. Contrast move_chat_page (019:98-108), which for the same kind of per-move data does check `exists(... rsvps r where r.user_id = auth.uid() and r.status='going') or exists(... moves mv where mv.creator_id = auth.uid())`.
findings.consequence: Today the exposure is bounded because no client path can create a private move (is_public defaults true, useCreateMove.ts never sets it), so every move's roster is already reachable through the world-readable rsvps table. The moment the is_public toggle ships — which the RLS policy at 004:78 is already built for — this function silently publishes the guest list of every private gathering to anyone holding the move id, which leaks through Share links (app/move/[id].tsx:60) and through /rest/v1/rsvps. A banned account (011:143-149 blocks it from reading the moves table) also retains full roster access through this RPC.
findings.fix: Add the visibility predicate that move_chat_page already uses. In a new migration, recreate get_move_attendees with `and exists (select 1 from public.moves mv where mv.id = p_move_id and (mv.is_public = true or mv.creator_id = auth.uid() or exists (select 1 from public.rsvps r2 where r2.move_id = p_move_id and r2.user_id = auth.uid() and r2.status = 'going')))` appended to the WHERE clause at 010:175.
findings.extra: Enforcement layer for move visibility inside get_move_attendees: NONE. Enforcement layer for blocks inside it: present (010:175) but bidirectional in the wrong direction — see the RSVP finding above.

Clean, and each was checked specifically rather than assumed:

REAL-TIME POSITION IS NEVER SENT TO THE SERVER. The core product claim holds at the schema level. There is no column anywhere in the 21 migrations that stores a user's device position — profiles (002, 007, 011, 020) has no geography column, and the only geography columns are moves.location_point (004:15) and spots.location_point (008:29), both creator-chosen destinations. The user's GPS fix is read in src/hooks/useLocation.ts:23 into a zustand store (src/store/locationStore.ts:18-23) that has no persist middleware, and leaves the device only as the ephemeral `lat`/`lng` RPC arguments in useNearbyMoves.ts:21-22 and app/(tabs)/index.tsx:72-73. Nothing writes it back. A stalker who fully compromises the database learns where people said they would be, not where anyone is.

MOVE CHAT IS BACKEND-ENFORCED AND STALE ACCESS IS REVOKED. The `isGoing || isCreator` gate at app/move/[id].tsx:282 is cosmetic, but it sits on top of two independent server checks that agree with it: the msg_select RLS policy (013_move_chat.sql:37-49) and the WHERE clause in move_chat_page (019_profiles_exposure.sql:98-108), both requiring a live `rsvps` row with status='going' or `moves.creator_id = auth.uid()`. Because both re-evaluate the rsvps row on every read rather than checking a membership snapshot, deleting your RSVP (useRSVP.ts leave path) revokes chat history immediately — including messages sent while you were a member. There is no invite/uninvite mechanism for moves, so there is no un-invite revocation path to test.

PRE-AUTH DEEP LINKS DO NOT LEAK MOVES. app/_layout.tsx:27-33 treats only `segments[0] === 'i'` as a public route; /move/[id] falls through to `router.replace('/(auth)/welcome')`. The redirect is in a useEffect so the screen mounts once first — but useMove (useMove.ts:42-48) reads `moves_with_counts`, which 015_security_hardening.sql:17 set to security_invoker=on, so RLS applies to that read and a private move would be denied. app/i/[code].tsx leaks nothing beyond invite-code validity, which is finding six's subject.

ON-DEVICE CACHING IS NOT A LEAK SURFACE. The only SecureStore keys are the Supabase auth session (src/lib/supabase.ts:5-9, :16-18) — encrypted at rest by the OS keychain/keystore. react-query has no persister configured (src/lib/queryClient.ts:3-17): gcTime is 10 minutes and lives in memory only, so nothing survives app termination. src/lib/storage.ts is an image uploader, not a cache. No AsyncStorage anywhere in src/ or app/.

public_profiles LEAKS NOTHING LOCATING. The ten columns (019:40-51) are id, username, display_name, avatar_url, bio, city, follower_count, following_count, moves_created, created_at. `city` is a text column defaulting to 'Pittsburgh' (002:8), city-granularity by construction. birthdate, social_handle, push_token, is_banned, banned_reason and referral_code are all correctly excluded, and the view filters is_banned=false. The exposure it does carry — that it is granted to anon (019:54) and so lets an unauthenticated caller resolve any username to a uuid — is the entry point for finding one, not a defect of the column list.

THE PREVIOUSLY-IDENTIFIED IDORs ARE ACTUALLY CLOSED. mark_activity_read no longer takes a target uuid (015:113-124, and the client comment at useActivity.ts:80-81 matches). promote_from_waitlist and recalc_hot_score have PUBLIC's default EXECUTE grant genuinely revoked (018:44-45, after 015:129's revoke-from-anon,authenticated was correctly diagnosed as a no-op). admin_ban_user/admin_unban_user are revoked from PUBLIC (020:58-59). profiles UPDATE is column-restricted (015:41-43), so is_banned and referral_code cannot be self-edited. blocked_either (010:29-37) is correctly SECURITY DEFINER — it has to be, since blocks_own_read (010:19-20) would otherwise hide the blocker_id=other_user direction from the caller.

findings.title: No in-app account deletion anywhere in the app or the schema — automatic rejection
findings.location: app/(tabs)/profile/index.tsx:161-174 (the only destructive action on the only settings surface is Sign out); supabase/migrations/001-020 (no delete/purge RPC exists); docs/legal/privacy-policy.md:52-54
findings.reproduction: Reviewer signs in, taps the Profile tab (app/(tabs)/_layout.tsx), scrolls to the bottom. The screen offers exactly three actions: Edit (line 64-75), Invite friends (line 113-134), Sign out (line 162-174). There is no Delete Account row, no Settings sub-screen, and no route in app/ that renders one. `grep -rniE "delete.?account|account.?deletion|delete_user" app/ src/ supabase/` returns zero hits outside the legal markdown. `grep -rniE "create (or replace )?function.*(delete|purge|erase|wipe)" supabase/migrations/*.sql` returns zero.
findings.consequence: Guideline 5.1.1(v) has been enforced for every app that supports account creation since 30 June 2022 and is one of the checks a reviewer performs first, because it takes ten seconds. This is a guaranteed first-submission rejection with a Resolution Center round-trip — call it 5-10 days of launch slip. It is aggravated by docs/legal/privacy-policy.md:52-54, which tells users "To delete your account and all associated data, email privacy@whatsthemove.app from your account email **or use the in-app option**" — a published claim about a feature that does not exist. Apple explicitly rejects email-only deletion paths, and a policy that promises an in-app option that is absent reads as a misrepresentation. DEPLOYMENT.md:110-112 audits the 1.2 checklist and never mentions 5.1.1(v), so the gap is not on the builder's radar.

findings.title: Privacy Policy and Terms exist as files but are unreachable from inside the app, and both carry an unfilled [DATE] placeholder

findings.title: Build declares two persistent-location Info.plist keys — one with Expo's generic boilerplate string — for an app that only ever requests foreground location
findings.location: app.json plugins block, expo-location entry (`locationAlwaysAndWhenInUsePermission`); node_modules/@expo/config-plugins/build/ios/Permissions.js:34; node_modules/expo-location/plugin/build/withLocation.js:21-29; src/hooks/useLocation.ts:15
findings.reproduction: Static trace of the config plugin. app.json passes only `locationAlwaysAndWhenInUsePermission` to expo-location. withLocation.js:21-24 calls `createPermissionsPlugin` with defaults for all three keys, including `NSLocationAlwaysUsageDescription: 'Allow $(PRODUCT_NAME) to access your location'`. Permissions.js:34 resolves each key as `permissions[k] || infoPlist[k] || description`. For `NSLocationAlwaysUsageDescription` the prop is undefined and app.json's `ios.infoPlist` does not set it, so the generic default is written into the built Info.plist verbatim. `NSLocationAlwaysAndWhenInUseUsageDescription` gets "WTM uses your location to show moves near you." Meanwhile the only location call in the entire client is `Location.requestForegroundPermissionsAsync()` at useLocation.ts:15 — `grep -rn requestBackgroundPermissionsAsync app/ src/` returns nothing, and no background task, geofence, or `UIBackgroundModes: location` exists.
findings.consequence: 5.1.1 rejection template: the binary declares persistent-location usage descriptions with no feature that requires persistent location. Compounding it, one of the two declared strings is Expo's untouched placeholder — "Allow What's The Move to access your location" states no purpose at all, which is precisely what 5.1.1's purpose-string requirement exists to catch. It also directly contradicts the app's own published policy: docs/legal/privacy-policy.md:25-26 lists "background location" under **What we do NOT collect**, and line 14-16 promises "We do **not** track location in the background." A reviewer comparing the Info.plist to the policy sees the binary asking for something the policy swears it never takes.
findings.fix:
In app.json, replace the expo-location plugin entry with:
```json
["expo-location", {
  "locationWhenInUsePermission": "WTM uses your location to show moves happening near you.",
  "locationAlwaysAndWhenInUsePermission": false,
  "locationAlwaysPermission": false
}]
```
`false` is the documented sentinel — Permissions.js:30-32 deletes the key from the Info.plist rather than writing a default. That leaves exactly one location key, matching the one call in useLocation.ts and the policy text.
findings.extra: Guideline 5.1.1 — purpose strings / persistent location justification

findings.title: The iOS location prompt fires at cold launch, before the welcome screen, before the user has an account
findings.location: app/_layout.tsx:15-21 (AuthGate calls useLocationInit() unconditionally in its body); src/hooks/useLocation.ts:9-11 (useEffect with empty deps → runs on first mount)
findings.reproduction: Delete and reinstall, launch the app. `RootLayout` renders `AuthGate` (line 87). `AuthGate` calls `useLocationInit()` at line 21 in its component body, before any auth branch — the `useEffect(() => { requestLocation(); }, [])` at useLocation.ts:9-11 fires on the first render, in parallel with the `useEffect` at _layout.tsx:23 that has not yet routed anywhere. The system location dialog appears over the splash/welcome screen. app/(auth)/welcome.tsx contains no location copy at all (`grep -niE 'location|permission' app/(auth)/welcome.tsx` matches only a `locations={[0,0.5,1]}` gradient prop), so there is no priming screen explaining the ask.
findings.consequence: 5.1.1 requires that data access be requested at the point it is needed and in context. A reviewer's first interaction with the build is a location prompt on a screen where they have not signed in, cannot see a map, and have no reason to grant it. Beyond the rejection risk, this is a measurable conversion cost: users who deny at cold launch are the ones you can never re-prompt without sending them to Settings, and the map tab (app/(tabs)/index.tsx) is the app's core surface. The prompt should fire when the map first needs coordinates, not before the account exists.
findings.fix: Move the call out of the root. Delete `useLocationInit();` from app/_layout.tsx:21 and call it inside app/(tabs)/index.tsx (the map screen) instead, so it fires only after the auth + age gates have passed. Better still, gate it behind an in-app priming card on the map: render the map at the Pittsburgh default (`app/(tabs)/create.tsx:107-108` already uses 40.4406/-79.9959 as the fallback) with a "Show moves near me" button that calls `requestLocation()` on tap.
findings.extra: Guideline 5.1.1 — request access in context, at the point of need

findings.title: Blocking a user does not hide their move-chat messages, and chat offers no path to block or report anyone
findings.location: supabase/migrations/019_profiles_exposure.sql:83-101 (move_chat_page has no blocked_either filter); src/components/moves/MoveChat.tsx:17-74 (MessageBubble renders no touchable); compare supabase/migrations/013_move_chat.sql:99, :152, :175 where blocked_either IS applied
findings.reproduction: User A and user B both RSVP 'going' to the same move. A opens A's profile of B (app/user/[id].tsx), taps the ellipsis, Block user, confirms. `useBlockUser` (useSafety.ts:33-36) inserts the row; B's moves and spots vanish from A's feeds because `nearby_moves` (013:99, 011:121), `nearby_spots` (013:152) and `get_move_attendees` (013:175) all end with `and not public.blocked_either(...)`. A then opens the shared move (app/move/[id].tsx:283) and scrolls to the chat. `move_chat_page` at 019:83-101 filters only on move_id and on whether the caller is going/creator — there is no `blocked_either` clause — so every message B has posted is still rendered, with B's avatar and @username. Every new message B sends also arrives live: the realtime handler at useMoveChat.ts:55-91 appends any INSERT on `move_messages` for that move with no block check. From that screen A has no recourse: MessageBubble (MoveChat.tsx:17-74) is a plain `<View>` with no onPress, so tapping the avatar or username does nothing and there is no route from chat to the profile that carries the block/report menu.
findings.consequence: Guideline 1.2 requires "a mechanism for users to block abusive users." The mechanism exists but stops at the one surface where harassment actually happens — a real-time group chat with people who have already agreed to meet at a physical location. A reviewer who tests block end-to-end (they do, for social apps) finds their blocked user still talking to them. Worse for the product than for the review: a user who blocks someone to escape harassment and then sees that person's messages keep arriving in the chat for a meetup they are both attending has been told the safety feature works when it does not. The block-confirm copy at app/user/[id].tsx:34 says "You won't see each other's moves, spots, or profiles" — technically accurate by omission, which is not a defence a reviewer accepts.
findings.fix: Two changes. (a) In supabase/migrations/019_profiles_exposure.sql:99, add the filter that every other feed function already has — after the closing paren of the visibility `and (...)` block and before `order by`, insert `and not public.blocked_either(m.user_id)`. (b) Make the author tappable so block/report is reachable from chat: in MoveChat.tsx, wrap the avatar+username in `<TouchableOpacity onPress={() => router.push(`/user/${msg.user_id}`)}>` (import `useRouter` from expo-router), which lands on app/user/[id].tsx where the existing ellipsis menu at line 156-163 already provides both Block and Report. Note (a) alone still leaves the block one-directional in the RPC's `security definer` context — verify blocked_either resolves auth.uid() correctly there, as it does in the 013 functions.
findings.extra: Guideline 1.2 — Safety, UGC, bullet 3 (block abusive users)

findings.title: Google Maps API key is a literal placeholder string in app.json — the app's primary tab is a Google-provider map
findings.location: app.json ios.config.googleMapsApiKey = "$(GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY)" and android.config.googleMaps.apiKey = "$(GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY)"; app/(tabs)/index.tsx:3 and :146 (`provider={PROVIDER_GOOGLE}`)
findings.reproduction: app.json is static JSON — Expo performs no environment interpolation on it (there is no app.config.js in the repo; `ls /home/user/wtm/wtm` shows app.json only). The string `$(GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY)` is written through verbatim: into Info.plist as `GMSApiKey` and into AndroidManifest as `com.google.android.geo.API_KEY`. On iOS, Xcode expands `$(VAR)` in Info.plist values against build settings; `GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY` is an EAS *environment variable* (DEPLOYMENT.md:79 sets it via `eas secret:create`), not an Xcode build setting, so it expands to empty. On Android there is no expansion mechanism at all and the literal string is passed to the Maps SDK. app/(tabs)/index.tsx:146 forces `provider={PROVIDER_GOOGLE}` on both platforms, so neither falls back to Apple Maps.
findings.consequence: The default tab — the map that is the entire product — renders as a grey grid with a Google watermark and no tiles, with markers floating on nothing. Guideline 2.1 App Completeness: a reviewer who opens the app and sees the core screen not working rejects without reading further, and the rejection note will be a screenshot of a blank map. This also invalidates the screenshot set DEPLOYMENT.md:101 plans to capture ('map, spots layer, ...').
findings.extra: Guideline 2.1 — App Completeness. Config defect is CONFIRMED from source; the exact blank-map rendering is HYPOTHESIS, unverifiable without a build.

findings.title: Privacy policy's "What we collect" list omits date of birth, which the app collects and stores
findings.location: docs/legal/privacy-policy.md:10-22 (the complete collection list); app/(auth)/verify-age.tsx:54-59 (writes birthdate to profiles); supabase/migrations/011_squad_safety.sql:10 (`birthdate date` column)
findings.reproduction: Read docs/legal/privacy-policy.md:10-22 — the five bullets are Account info (email, username, display name, photo, bio), Location, Content you post, Invite graph, Device info (push token, diagnostics). Date of birth appears in none of them. Now trace app/(auth)/verify-age.tsx: line 54 computes `birthdateFor(selected, hadBirthday)` → a real date string, line 56-59 `supabase.from('profiles').update({ birthdate }).eq('id', profile.id)`. The value persists in `profiles.birthdate` (011:10) and drives the `set_age_range` trigger (011:17-34), which stores a derived `age_range` ('17-20' / '21-25') alongside it. The age gate is mandatory — app/_layout.tsx:42-45 routes any profile without a birthdate to verify-age and will not let them past.
findings.consequence: 5.1.1(i) requires the privacy policy to "clearly and explicitly identify what data the app collects." Date of birth is a category Apple's own nutrition-label taxonomy calls out separately, and for a 17-25 app it is the single most sensitive field collected — it is the basis of the eligibility gate. A reviewer cross-checking the App Store Connect nutrition label against the linked policy finds a field the policy does not mention. Independently, DEPLOYMENT.md:102-103 plans the nutrition label as "location, user content, identifiers (push token)" — birthdate is missing there too, so the label will be filed inaccurate, which Apple treats as a metadata violation and can act on after approval.
findings.fix: Add a bullet to docs/legal/privacy-policy.md after line 13: `- **Date of birth** — collected once at signup to enforce the 17-25 age requirement. We store the date and a derived age band; we do not use it for anything else.` Then add "Contact Info → Other User Contact Info / Sensitive Info" or, more precisely, the Date of Birth entry to the App Store Connect nutrition label, and amend the DEPLOYMENT.md:102-103 checklist line to match.
findings.extra: Guideline 5.1.1(i) — privacy policy completeness / nutrition label accuracy

findings.title: Push notification stack is declared and consumed server-side but no client code ever obtains a token — push_token is永 null
findings.location: app.json plugins: ["expo-notifications", {...}]; supabase/functions/daily-digest/index.ts:88-101 (selects push_token, posts to Expo); supabase/migrations/002_auth_profiles.sql:8 (`push_token text`); no producer anywhere in app/ or src/
findings.reproduction: `grep -rnE "getExpoPushTokenAsync|Notifications\.requestPermissionsAsync|getDevicePushTokenAsync" app/ src/` returns zero. `grep -rn push_token app/ src/` returns only the two type declarations (src/types/database.ts:24, src/types/app.ts:23) — no read, no write. The only write grant exists (015_security_hardening.sql:42 grants update on push_token) but nothing exercises it. daily-digest/index.ts:88-89 then runs `.select('push_token, username').not('push_token','is',null)` and line 101 sends `to: u.push_token`. Because nothing ever populates the column, that filter matches zero rows on every run.
findings.consequence: Three concrete costs. (1) The daily digest — the retention mechanism DEPLOYMENT.md treats as shipped — sends nothing, forever, silently. (2) The app declares the expo-notifications plugin, which adds the `aps-environment` entitlement and a push capability to a binary with no notification feature; reviewers do ask what the push capability is for. (3) docs/legal/privacy-policy.md:21 tells users the app collects "a push notification token (if you enable notifications)" and there is no enable path, and DEPLOYMENT.md:102-103 plans to declare "identifiers (push token)" on the nutrition label — declaring collection of data the binary never collects is the inverse of the usual label error but still an inaccurate label.
findings.fix: Either implement or remove — do not ship the half. To implement: in app/_layout.tsx, after the profile exists (inside the AuthGate effect, after line 45), call `const { status } = await Notifications.requestPermissionsAsync(); if (status === 'granted') { const t = (await Notifications.getExpoPushTokenAsync({ projectId })).data; await supabase.from('profiles').update({ push_token: t }).eq('id', profile.id); }` — note this must be a user-visible opt-in, not silent, and `projectId` requires fixing the placeholder in app.json's extra.eas block. To remove: delete the expo-notifications plugin entry from app.json, delete supabase/functions/daily-digest, and drop the push_token bullet from privacy-policy.md:21 and the nutrition-label line in DEPLOYMENT.md:103.
findings.extra: Nutrition-label accuracy (5.1.1(i)) plus a dead retention feature. Not a standalone rejection on its own.

findings.title: Camera permission declared on both platforms; no code path ever opens the camera
findings.location: app.json ios.infoPlist.NSCameraUsageDescription and android.permissions["CAMERA"]; the three image entry points are app/(tabs)/create.tsx:84-94, app/(tabs)/profile/edit.tsx:22, app/add-spot.tsx:37 — all `launchImageLibraryAsync`
findings.reproduction: `grep -rnE "launchCameraAsync|requestCameraPermissionsAsync" app/ src/` returns zero hits. All three image flows call `ImagePicker.launchImageLibraryAsync` only, which needs NSPhotoLibraryUsageDescription and nothing else. app.json nonetheless declares `NSCameraUsageDescription: "WTM needs camera access to take a photo for your move."` and lists `CAMERA` in android.permissions; separately, node_modules/expo-image-picker/plugin/build/withImagePicker.js:26-32 would default-fill NSCameraUsageDescription anyway since `cameraPermission` is not passed. There is also no UI affordance offering "Take a photo" — pickImage in create.tsx:84 goes straight to the library with no action sheet.
findings.consequence: Apple's automated purpose-string check does not reject for a declared-but-unfired string, so the iOS rejection probability here is genuinely low — I am reporting it because it is provable and cheap, not because it will bounce the build. The real exposure is Google Play, where a declared CAMERA permission with no camera feature draws a policy flag, as does READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE / WRITE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE in the same android.permissions array (both are obsolete on API 33+ and expo-image-picker does not need them).
findings.fix: In app.json: delete the `NSCameraUsageDescription` line from ios.infoPlist, and pass `"cameraPermission": false` in the expo-image-picker plugin options so withImagePicker does not write its default back in. Trim android.permissions to `["ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION", "ACCESS_COARSE_LOCATION"]` — CAMERA, READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE and WRITE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE are all unused. Alternatively, if a camera capture flow is intended, add an action sheet to pickImage offering `launchCameraAsync`, which makes all three declarations legitimate.
findings.extra: Guideline 5.1.1 — declared-but-unused permissions. Low Apple risk, real Google Play risk.

findings.title: hot_score is the feed's sort key and one self-RSVP on a soon-starting move beats every genuinely popular move
findings.location: supabase/migrations/016_one_nearby_moves.sql:131 (order by m.hot_score desc, m.starts_at asc) + supabase/migrations/012_activity_momentum.sql:20,28-32 (recalc_hot_score) + src/hooks/useCreateMove.ts:38-42 (creator auto-RSVP)
findings.reproduction: With an account older than 24h (011:126 cooldown), open the Create tab. Title anything, pick a category, type a location, set the start time to 15 minutes from now, toggle "Limit spots" on and set it to 1, tap "Post it". useCreateMove inserts an rsvps row for the creator (line 38), which fires rsvp_hot_score -> recalc_hot_score. v_hours = greatest(0.25, 0.25) = 0.25, v_count = 1, v_cap = 1, so hot_score = 1/0.25 * (1 + 1/1) = 8.0. Repeat 20 times — nothing in the schema rate-limits move creation past the one-time 24h new-account cooldown, and moves_authenticated_insert / moves_insert only check creator_id = auth.uid().
findings.consequence: A real move 6 hours out with 20 of 30 spots filled scores 20/6 * (1 + 20/30) = 5.6 and loses to a fake move with one attendee. Twenty junk posts own the entire first page of nearby_moves for every user within the 8047 m radius. Without the capacity cap the same move scores 1/0.25 = 4.0, which clears MoveCard.tsx:38 HOT_THRESHOLD = 1.5, so it also renders the "🔥 Trending" badge on a move with literally one person going. This is free top-of-feed placement for anyone bored enough to tap Post twenty times, in the one surface the whole product depends on.
findings.fix: In 012_activity_momentum.sql, damp the imminence term and require real signal: at line 20 raise the floor from 0.25 to 2.0 (`greatest(2.0, extract(epoch from (m.starts_at - now())) / 3600.0)`) so a 15-minute-out move is not worth 4x, and at line 29 subtract the creator's own RSVP (`greatest(0, v_count - 1)::numeric / v_hours`) so a self-RSVP scores zero. Separately add a per-creator creation limit as a RESTRICTIVE insert policy on moves: `(select count(*) from public.moves where creator_id = auth.uid() and created_at > now() - interval '1 hour') < 5`.
findings.extra: No rate limit exists anywhere in the repo except 011:126 (one-time 24h new-account cooldown) and a 500 ms map-pan debounce at app/(tabs)/index.tsx:105.

findings.title: A move ending after midnight is rejected with a raw Postgres error — the default case for a nightlife app
findings.location: app/(tabs)/create.tsx:361-365 (end picker, mode="time", date={form.endsAt ?? form.startsAt}) and :98-116 (handleSubmit, no time comparison) + supabase/migrations/004_moves.sql:35 (ends_after_starts)
findings.reproduction: Create tab -> set start to Fri 11:00 PM -> toggle "Set end time" -> tap "Pick end time" -> choose 1:00 AM -> tap "Post it". The end picker is mode="time" seeded with `date={form.endsAt ?? form.startsAt}`, so the calendar date it carries is the START's date; the confirm handler at :364 writes the returned Date straight into form.endsAt with no adjustment, and there is no next-day roll and no start-vs-end comparison anywhere in the file. ends_at = Fri 1:00 AM, 22 hours before starts_at. 004:35 `check (ends_at is null or ends_at > starts_at)` rejects the insert.

This is not an edge case: it is the shape of essentially every bar crawl, house party and late show in a 17-25 nightlife app, i.e. the app's core use case fails closed with a database error string. findings.extra: Enforcement layer: DB CHECK 004:35 only. No client-side comparison exists in create.tsx.

findings.title: An emoji display name renders a broken-glyph avatar; a zero-width display name renders an invisible identity

findings.reproduction: (a) Profile -> Edit -> DISPLAY NAME -> type a single emoji, e.g. 🎉 (U+1F389) -> Save. `display_name.trim()` at edit.tsx:47 leaves it intact; profiles.display_name has no format constraint (unlike profiles.username, which 002:18 pins to ^[a-z0-9_]{3,20}$). Tap "Join Move" / "You're in" alternately, waiting for the spinner each time (RSVPButton.tsx:96 disables the button while any of the four mutations is pending, so pure spam-tapping is correctly absorbed — this is the loop that is not). 200 cycles takes a few minutes of thumb work. Each successful INSERT fires notify_creator_on_rsvp, which at 012:86 does a bare `insert into public.activity_feed(...)` with no ON CONFLICT and no time window; 015:178-184 explicitly documents that no unique index exists on activity_feed and that adding one was deliberately rejected. In app/move/[id].tsx:44-52, coalesce the realtime storm: hold a `useRef<ReturnType<typeof setTimeout>>()` and replace the handler body with `clearTimeout(t.current); t.current = setTimeout(() => { queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: queryKeys.moves.detail(id) }); queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: queryKeys.rsvps.forMove(id) }); }, 400);`

findings.title: The create form is never reset after a successful post, so returning to the tab and tapping again duplicates the move

findings.title: Cold launch with a failed profile fetch strands the user inside the app with the 17–25 age gate skipped, and nothing ever retries
findings.location: src/hooks/useSession.ts:32-40 and app/_layout.tsx:23-50 (guard at :39)
findings.reproduction: Sign up, force-quit before completing verify-age (or just have any existing user). Relaunch on a dead/captive-portal connection (subway, plane wifi). getSession() resolves from SecureStore (session persists), fetchProfile() runs `.select('*').eq('id',...).single()`, the request fails, and the destructure `const { data } = ...` discards the error and calls setProfile(null) with setLoading(false). AuthGate then runs: isLoading false, isAuthenticated true, `if (!profile) return;` at _layout.tsx:39 — it returns before both the age gate (:42) and the leave-auth-group redirect (:48). No navigation happens, so the router stays on '/' which resolves to app/(tabs)/index.tsx (the map).
findings.consequence: The user lands in the full tab UI as an authenticated member with profile === null and birthdate never checked. fetchProfile is only ever called from the two branches in the useEffect at useSession.ts:9-30, so when connectivity returns nothing re-fetches — the state persists for the whole app run and repeats on every launch that hits the same condition. Net effect: an age-unverified account gets unrestricted access to a 17–25-only social app, indefinitely, with no visible error. The same terminal state occurs if the profile row is genuinely missing (handle_new_user trigger failure), which is the 'auth account but no profile row' case: there is no sign-out affordance reachable from the tabs to escape it.
findings.fix: In useSession.ts:32-40 capture the error and distinguish the two cases: `const { data, error } = await supabase.from('profiles')...; if (error) { setProfileError(error); setLoading(false); return; } setProfile(data ?? null);`. In app/_layout.tsx replace the bare `if (!profile) return;` at :39 with a branch that (a) renders a blocking retry screen when the fetch errored, and (b) routes to /(auth)/verify-age (or signs out) when the fetch succeeded and returned no row — never silently falls through to the tabs.
findings.extra: Answers the brief's question directly: yes, a user can be age-unverified forever, and yes, an auth account with no profile row is a terminal state.

findings.title: Global mutation `retry: 1` turns a dropped response into a duplicate move or duplicate chat message
findings.location: src/lib/queryClient.ts:13-15; src/hooks/useCreateMove.ts:14-34; src/hooks/useMoveChat.ts:104-114
findings.reproduction: On a flaky connection (train, elevator, 1-bar LTE), tap 'Post it' on app/(tabs)/create.tsx. The POST to /rest/v1/moves reaches Postgres and commits, then the TCP connection drops before the response returns. fetch rejects, mutationFn throws, and react-query's default `mutations: { retry: 1 }` re-runs the whole mutationFn — including the `.insert(...)` at useCreateMove.ts:15-32. Verified against query-core/build/modern/mutation.js: onMutate is awaited once at L102, then `retryer.start()` at L115 retries only mutationFn, so the write body is replayed verbatim.
findings.consequence: Two identical moves in the feed, both with the creator auto-RSVP'd, both visible to every nearby user; the creator only sees the second one (router.replace to the returned id) and has no idea the first exists. moves has no idempotency key and no unique constraint that would catch it (supabase/migrations/004_moves.sql:13-37). Same mechanism duplicates a chat message (useMoveChat.ts:106-109). For rsvps the retry instead hits `unique(move_id,user_id)` (005_rsvps.sql:10) and returns 23505, so the user is told the join failed while the row exists.
findings.fix: Set `mutations: { retry: 0 }` in src/lib/queryClient.ts:13-15 — non-idempotent writes must not be blind-retried. If retry is wanted for the RSVP path only, make the write idempotent first: `.upsert({...}, { onConflict: 'move_id,user_id' })` in useRSVP.ts:34-36, and add a client-generated `id: uuid` to the moves and move_messages inserts so a replay collides on the primary key instead of creating a second row.

findings.title: 'Cancel this move' throws its error away — the creator is told it worked and walks off while attendees still show up

Line 79 is `await supabase.from('moves').update({ is_cancelled: true }).eq('id', id);` with no destructure and no error check. findings.title: The whole Supabase session is written to expo-secure-store, whose documented value limit is 2048 bytes
findings.location: src/lib/supabase.ts:5-21
findings.reproduction: Sign in, force-quit, relaunch. The adapter at :5-9 hands the entire serialized session (access JWT + refresh token + full user object + user_metadata) to SecureStore.setItemAsync as one value. node_modules/expo-secure-store/build/SecureStore.js:151-152 warns above VALUE_BYTES_LIMIT = 2048 ('may not be stored successfully'). A Supabase HS256 session JSON routinely exceeds that once user_metadata carries username, display_name and invite_code_id (set at sign-up.tsx:69-75).
findings.consequence: If the write is dropped, getSession() returns null on relaunch, AuthGate routes to /(auth)/welcome (_layout.tsx:33), and the user must sign in again on every cold start — in an invite-only app where many users no longer have their password saved. Failure is silent: the adapter returns the promise unchecked and nothing logs.
findings.fix: Either move the session to AsyncStorage (`@react-native-async-storage/async-storage`, which has no per-value limit) and keep SecureStore only if a hardware-backed store is a requirement, or chunk in the adapter: split the value into 1800-byte parts under `${key}.0`, `${key}.1`, … plus a count key, and reassemble in getItem. Also stop shipping non-essential fields in `options.data` at sign-up.tsx:69-75.
findings.extra: CONFIRMED by reading: the full session goes to SecureStore unchunked, and the installed module documents a 2048-byte ceiling. Whether a given session actually exceeds it, and whether the platform silently drops or throws, needs a device run — hence HYPOTHESIS on the outcome.

findings.title: Social proof (crew_going) reads invite_codes.used_by, which records only the FIRST redeemer of a 5-use code — so users 2 through 5 of any code have an empty friend graph in both directions
findings.location: supabase/migrations/016_one_nearby_moves.sql:104-110; supabase/migrations/007_referrals.sql:60,78-79; supabase/migrations/015_security_hardening.sql:97-99
findings.reproduction: 007_referrals.sql:78-79 mints each new member one invite_codes row with `max_uses = public.default_invite_allowance()` = 5 (line 18). findings.title: validate-invite is an unauthenticated, unthrottled oracle over a 1,048,576-key space — the invite wall is scriptable
findings.location: supabase/functions/validate-invite/index.ts:9-59 (no rate limit, no per-IP counter, no state); supabase/migrations/007_referrals.sql:25-35 (generate_referral_code builds 'MOVE' + 4 chars from a 32-character alphabet)
findings.reproduction: The function's only gate is a well-formed JSON body. Auth is the anon key, which ships inside the app bundle (src/lib/supabase.ts:12, EXPO_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY). The response distinguishes outcomes precisely: `{valid:false,reason:'not_found'}` at :36-39 vs `{valid:true,codeId}` at :56-59. A loop of `curl -s -X POST https://<ref>.supabase.co/functions/v1/validate-invite -H 'apikey: <anon>' -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"code":"MOVE"+<4 random chars from ABCDEFGHJKLMNPQRSTUVWXYZ23456789>}'` enumerates the entire personal-code space. Supporting detail: the invite screen's own placeholder text is 'e.g. PITTSB42' (app/(auth)/invite.tsx:90) and supabase/seed.sql:4-9 seeds PITTSB01, PITTSB02, STEEL412, YINZER22, DEVBETA1 with max_uses 50-100 — the placeholder advertises the seeded pattern.
findings.consequence: The invite-only wall is the product's entire premise and its only Trust & Safety control on a 17-25 app. With M members each holding one live MOVE code, the expected number of guesses to a hit is ~1,048,576/M — at 200 members roughly 5,200 requests. Nothing in the function or in supabase/config.toml throttles that. A stranger walks past the age gate and the vetting story that the ToS and the App Store review notes both lean on. Secondary cost: each guess is one Edge Function invocation plus one Postgres round trip against the free tier's 500K/month invocation budget.
findings.fix: Three changes, all small. (a) supabase/migrations/021: widen the suffix in generate_referral_code from `for i in 1..4` to `for i in 1..8` — the code_format CHECK already permits 12 characters (003:10) — taking the space to 32^8 ≈ 1.1e12. (b) In validate-invite/index.ts, before the lookup at :29, insert into a new `public.invite_attempts(ip text, created_at timestamptz default now())` keyed on `req.headers.get('x-forwarded-for')` and return 429 when that IP has more than 10 failures in the last 10 minutes. (c) After the third miss from an IP, collapse the response to a bare `{valid:false}` with no `reason` field so the endpoint stops distinguishing 'not_found' from 'used' from 'expired'.
findings.extra: The 1,048,576 key-space arithmetic and the total absence of throttling are both provable from source. The wall-clock time to a hit depends on Supabase's platform-level edge limits, which are not in this repo — treat the 'under a minute' figure as HYPOTHESIS; the exploitability is not.

findings.title: DELETE: three permissions the app never exercises, one of which contradicts the product's own positioning

findings.title: A banned or deleted account silently empties its invitees' only social graph, with no reassignment and no explanation
findings.location: supabase/migrations/003_invite_codes.sql:4-5 and 007_referrals.sql:11 (all invite edges are `on delete set null`); supabase/migrations/016_one_nearby_moves.sql:104-110 and 014:125-135 (crew_going derives 'friends' exclusively from invite_codes.created_by/used_by); 019_profiles_exposure.sql:52 (public_profiles filters is_banned)

Now: nearby_moves excludes every move A created (`creator.is_banned = false`, 016:128); A vanishes from public_profiles (019:52) so B tapping A's avatar gets the 'User not found' branch at app/user/[id].tsx:110-116; and because B's only invite-graph edge was to A, the crew_going subquery (016:104-110) returns [] on every card B ever sees. The 'N from your crew are going' row that migration 016 exists to produce goes dark for that member forever, and the app just looks broken rather than moderated. Separately, app/user/[id].tsx:110-116 currently renders a bare 'User not found' — change it to 'This account is no longer on WTM' so a removed member reads as removed, not as a bug.
